title: Unsecured Credentials
summary: This parent technique covers credential collection that requires no memory access and no cryptographic attack, because the secret was simply left readable. Adversaries enumerate a compromised host for the places administrators and applications habitually store secrets: plaintext notes and configuration files, script and command history, registry values, unprotected private keys, and cloud metadata endpoints. In each case the credential is available to a process that only needs read access, and often to any local user. The defining artefact is an access pattern rather than a file: broad or targeted reads during the search phase, frequently by an interpreter, archive utility or scripting host rather than the application that legitimately owns the file. Discovered credentials are then used directly or added to an offline cracking queue. Detection depends on command-line and process creation logging, which for Windows includes security event 4688 and Sysmon event 1, plus file access auditing on the directories where secrets usually live. Because legitimate backup and configuration tooling touches the same paths, volume and actor baseline matter more than a single hit.

beginner.definition: People often leave passwords where anyone can read them, such as notes, setup files, or saved keys. This parent technique is when an attacker searches a computer for those loose secrets instead of stealing them from memory. It needs no clever trick, only patience and read access.
beginner.whyItMatters: One readable file can unlock a database, a cloud account, or every server the team manages. The attacker does not need to break any protection, so there is nothing to patch. Mistakes like this are common because saving a password in a file is convenient.
howItWorks: An attacker gets a foothold on a machine, often with an ordinary user account.
They look through the common places where people save passwords and keys.
They read setup files, scripts, notes, and temporary folders while hunting for secrets.
They may collect command history, which records the commands other users typed.
They search the system registry or operating system stores for saved values.
Every secret found is tried against other systems, extending the attacker's reach.
beginner.example: Think of an office where the cleaner is allowed in every room at night. One desk has the safe combination written on a sticky note under the keyboard. The cleaner never touches the safe, opens nothing by force, and takes only a photograph of the note. The building is still locked. The secret was simply lying in the open.
takeaways: Search your systems for stored secrets before an attacker does.
Never place passwords or keys in notes, scripts, or setup files.
Track who reads sensitive folders, and alert when the reader is unexpected.

objectives: List the common locations where credentials are stored insecurely.
Explain why this technique needs no memory access or password cracking.
Describe the search behaviour that precedes discovery of a stored secret.
Identify the log sources that record file and registry read activity.
Explain how to prioritise secret storage risks during a review.
